value: prey triggered the trap directly with one of its second antennae in 12 of 14 prey capture attempts (~86%)
method: high-speed video of single isolated traps in cuvettes triggered by swimming prey (Daphnia longicephala); prey capture attempts (PCAs) counted
conditions: Australian (tropical) ecotype from Girraween Lagoon, Northern Territory, plants from a living collection in the Czech Republic; one trap per attempt, traps were seventh-whorl leaves cut under water without being triggered and held in a polystyrene cuvette with 3 ml of water and prey at 24 °C; prey were 3-6 day old Daphnia longicephala clones; n = 14 attempts. Same results section: in one attempt (about 7%) the prey triggered the trap with its tail spine, and prey was caught in 9 of the 14 attempts (~64%) while in the other five the traps were triggered but nothing was caught. The paper reports prey triggering by touching the trigger hairs; it does not measure a touch threshold. No correlation was found between prey density and time to triggering (Spearman rho 0.028, p = 0.92).

value: highest tentacle bending speed in the study, median 7.38 °/s, in mechanically stimulated snap-tentacles
method: tentacles touched with an inert platinum needle held in a micromanipulator, at the gland head and on the stalk; bending angle over time from video; a tentacle counted as responding if it moved within 5-7 min
conditions: snap-tentacles (bilaterally symmetrical gland heads at the leaf margin); Table 1 lists for mechanically stimulated D. allantostigma snap-tentacles a response rate of 31.2% (95% CI 20.9-41.5%), median response time 17.5 s and angular velocity quartiles 1.0 and 15.8 °/s; peripheral tentacles responded more often (56.8%) but more slowly (median 4.08 °/s). Plants kept at 23 °C in greenhouses, 56 trap-leaves from 21 rosettes in all (22 mechanical stimuli). For comparison the paper's slowest value was in mechanically stimulated snap-tentacles of D. rotundifolia (0.65 °/s). Chemical (fish food) stimulation of D. allantostigma snap-tentacles gave 49.1% response and a median 3.41 °/s. The paper does not give the force applied by the needle and plant age is not stated.

value: touch-induced cytosolic Ca2+ signal and action potential propagated along the rachilla at 5.87 ± 0.75 and 5.52 ± 0.43 mm/s, respectively
method: leaf pinna tip touched with forceps while cytosolic Ca2+ (GCaMP6f imaging) and surface potential (two extracellular Ag/AgCl electrodes on the rachilla) were recorded together
conditions: transgenic Mimosa pudica expressing LjUBQ1p::GCaMP6f (Agrobacterium-mediated transformation); grown in a chamber at 27/20 °C day/night, 12 h light / 12 h dark; touch by tweezers or a pipette tip with no force or duration given; the Figure 2 legend gives no n for the touch recordings and the values come from Supplementary Table 1 (not seen). Wounding with scissors gave slower propagation, 4.13 ± 0.45 (Ca2+) and 4.27 ± 0.41 mm/s (AP), and a second wound-induced variation potential. The paper reports that touch-evoked leaflet movement stays within the touched pinna because the action potential cannot cross the secondary pulvinus, and its model of touch sensing as a herbivore defence rests partly on La3+ pharmacology and 'should be validated in the field'.
